name: Honey
habitat: Not foraged so much as kept, traded, or robbed from a wild colony. Included because it is the strongest wound antiseptic in this corpus that a person plausibly has.
identify: Raw, unpasteurised honey is the useful kind; heat and filtration reduce the activity.
Medical-grade and manuka honeys are the standardised versions of the same thing.

preparations.method: Spread a layer of honey on a clean dressing rather than pouring it into the wound, and apply. Change when it has been diluted by wound fluid — often daily at first.
preparations.for_use: Burns, ulcers, and slow-healing or infected wounds. It draws fluid out osmotically, produces hydrogen peroxide slowly, is too sugar-dense for bacteria to grow in, and keeps the dressing from sticking.

cautions: NEVER give honey to an infant under one year old — botulism spores that an adult gut handles can germinate in an infant's, and it is fatal.
Wild honey from rhododendron, azalea or mountain laurel nectar can be 'mad honey' carrying grayanotoxin, which causes dizziness, vomiting, low heart rate and collapse.
It is a dressing, not a substitute for irrigation and for medical care in a serious wound.
Robbing a wild colony is dangerous in its own right and destroys the colony.
evidence: The best-evidenced entry here: honey dressings for burns and wounds are supported by clinical trials and Cochrane review, and medical-grade honey is in routine hospital use.
